title: 22. Interview: WebSockets
summary: Interview Q&A for WebSockets — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 WebSockets interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is a WebSocket, and how does it differ from HTTP?
**Answer:** A WebSocket is a full-duplex, persistent, bidirectional communication channel that begins life as an HTTP Upgrade request and then becomes a frame-based protocol over the same TCP connection. The client opens with a normal HTTP GET carrying `Upgrade: websocket` and a random `Sec-WebSocket-Key`; the server responds with `101 Switching Protocols` and a `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` value derived from a SHA-1 of the key plus a fixed magic GUID. From that byte onward the connection is no longer HTTP — both sides may send opcode-tagged frames (text, binary, ping, pong, close) at any time, with 2-14 byte headers per frame. Differences from HTTP: (1) **Direction** — HTTP is strictly request-response (client asks, server answers); WebSocket is bidirectional (either side sends at any time). (2) **Persistence** — HTTP/1.1 typically closes or pools a request per resource; WebSocket is one long-lived connection. (3) **Overhead** — HTTP repeats headers on every request (~200-800 bytes); WebSocket frames are 2-14 bytes. (4) **Server push** — HTTP has no native server push (workarounds: long polling, SSE); WebSocket does it natively. (5) **Use case** — HTTP for request-response CRUD; WebSocket for chat, multiplayer, live dashboards. WhatsApp, Slack, Discord, and Figma all use WebSockets for real-time push.
**Visual:**
```
HTTP:        client --req--> server --resp--> client  (close)
WebSocket:   client --Upgrade--> server --101--> client
             (TCP now bidirectional)
             client <----> server  (frames any time, any direction)
```

### Q2. Walk me through the WebSocket handshake step by step.
**Answer:** Step 1: The client sends a normal HTTP GET to the WebSocket URL (`ws://` or `wss://`) with headers `Upgrade: websocket`, `Connection: Upgrade`, `Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13`, and `Sec-WebSocket-Key` set to 16 random bytes base64-encoded (e.g., `dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==`). Step 2: The server validates the headers and, if it accepts the upgrade, computes `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` = base64(SHA1(client_key + "258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B11")). The magic GUID proves the server actually understood the protocol (defense against confused-deputy attacks where a non-WebSocket server just echoes headers). Step 3: The server responds with HTTP `101 Switching Protocols`, headers `Upgrade: websocket`, `Connection: Upgrade`, and the computed accept value. Step 4: The TCP connection is now upgraded — neither side sends HTTP anymore. Both sides exchange binary WebSocket frames per RFC 6455. Step 5: To close, either side sends a close frame (opcode 0x8) with a status code (1000 normal, 1001 going away, 1011 internal error); the other side echoes a close frame back, then TCP teardown follows. The whole handshake is one HTTP round trip — after that, every message is one TCP round trip with no per-message TLS or HTTP overhead.
**Visual:**
```
client                               server
  |  GET /chat HTTP/1.1                |
  |  Upgrade: websocket                |
  |  Connection: Upgrade               |
  |  Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhl...        |
  |  Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13         |
  |----------------------------------->|
  |  HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols  |
  |  Upgrade: websocket                |
  |  Connection: Upgrade               |
  |  Sec-WebSocket-Accept: s3pP...     |
  |<-----------------------------------|
  |  (TCP socket now speaks WebSocket) |
  |<=== bidirectional frames ========>|
```

### Q3. What are the WebSocket frame opcodes, and why are ping/pong frames important?
**Answer:** RFC 6455 defines six opcodes: `0x0` continuation (for fragmented messages), `0x1` text (UTF-8 payload), `0x2` binary (raw bytes), `0x8` close (carries status code + reason), `0x9` ping (control, 0-125 byte payload), `0xA` pong (control, mirrors ping payload). Text and binary are the data opcodes; close, ping, pong are control opcodes that must be processed even mid-fragmented-message. Ping/pong matters for three reasons. First, **liveness detection** — TCP keepalive defaults to 2 hours on Linux, which is far too slow for real-time apps; WebSocket apps send ping every 20-30 seconds and expect a pong within a few seconds; a missed pong means the client is dead (battery died, NAT dropped the mapping, network changed) and the server closes the socket to free resources. Second, **NAT/firewall keep-alive** — many NATs and corporate firewalls drop idle TCP connections after 30-60 seconds; periodic pings keep the connection visible. Third, **back-pressure signaling** — a server can delay its pong to signal congestion, though this is rarely used in practice. WhatsApp, Slack, and Discord all rely on ping/pong to detect dead sockets; without it, servers would accumulate ghost connections that never time out, leaking file descriptors and memory.
**Visual:**
```
server ---ping (0x9)--> client      every 30s
client ---pong (0xA)--> server      within 5s

if pong not received within timeout:
  server closes socket (1006 abnormal) -> free fd + memory
```

### Q4. How do you scale WebSocket servers horizontally?
**Answer:** Scaling WebSockets is fundamentally harder than scaling stateless HTTP because each connection is stateful — the user's session, subscriptions, and any in-flight messages live on one specific server. The recipe has four parts. (1) **Sticky load balancing** — the L7 load balancer (HAProxy, NGINX, AWS ALB, Cloudflare) routes the initial HTTP Upgrade request to a backend, then pins that TCP connection to that backend for its lifetime. A session cookie or hash of the user_id ensures reconnecting clients land on the same node holding their state. (2) **Pub/sub fan-out** — when server A wants to push to user X whose socket lives on server B, A publishes the event to a shared Redis/Kafka/NATS pub-sub channel that every WebSocket node subscribes to; node B receives the event and writes it to X's socket. Discord uses roughly this pattern at scale, with a sharded gateway fronting Redis pub-sub. (3) **Heartbeats and timeouts** — ping every 30s, close sockets that miss two pongs; otherwise ghost connections accumulate. (4) **Connection draining** — when a node is being decommissioned, the load balancer stops sending new connections, the server sends close frames with `1001 Going Away` to existing clients, clients auto-reconnect to a new node, and the new node fetches the user's session from Redis to resume. WhatsApp and Slack both implement resume with sequence numbers so a reconnect doesn't lose messages.
**Visual:**
```
                    +------------------+
   client1 -------> | Load Balancer    | (sticky: hash(user_id))
                    +--------+---------+
            __________________|___________________
           /         |                     |
       +--+--+   +---+---+             +---+---+
       | ws1 |   | ws2   |             | ws3   |
       +--+--+   +---+---+             +---+---+
          |         |                     |
          +---------+----+ <Redis> ------+
                     |  pub/sub fan-out  |
                     +-------------------+
   server A wants to push to user X on ws2:
     A -> Redis PUBLISH user_X {"msg":"hi"}
     ws2 (subscribed to user_X) -> writes frame to X's socket
```

### Q5. What is the difference between WebSockets, SSE, and long polling?
**Answer:** All three solve server push, but with very different trade-offs. **Long polling** — client sends HTTP GET, server holds the request open up to 30s waiting for data, then responds; client immediately re-requests. Simple, works everywhere (even ancient proxies), but high overhead (fresh HTTP request per event batch, thread per held request on server), and high latency for the first event after a poll cycle. **SSE (Server-Sent Events)** — client opens a single long-lived HTTP GET to `/stream`; server pushes `text/event-stream` chunks using the standard `EventSource` browser API. Unidirectional (server to client only), auto-reconnects with `Last-Event-ID`, simple, but client cannot send messages back (must use a separate HTTP POST). **WebSocket** — full-duplex, bidirectional, low per-frame overhead, server can push and client can push at any time. Highest capability and lowest latency, but most complex: sticky sessions, custom back-pressure, manual reconnection logic, harder to debug (binary frames, no `curl`). Decision tree: need bidirectional (chat, multiplayer) → WebSocket. Need server-to-client only (live feed, notifications, ChatGPT token streaming) → SSE. Need to support legacy proxies or simple servers (early 2000s Gmail chat) → long polling. Discord, WhatsApp, Slack, Figma all use WebSockets; Twitter live feed and ChatGPT token streaming use SSE.
**Visual:**
```
Long polling:    client --req--> server (hold 30s) --resp--> client --req--> ...
SSE:             client --req--> server (one long-lived HTTP stream)
                 client <--event-- server (pushes text/event-stream chunks)
                 client <--event-- server (auto-reconnect with Last-Event-ID)
WebSocket:       client --Upgrade--> server --101--> (bidirectional)
                 client <--frame--> server (text, binary, ping/pong any time)
```

### Q6. What is the masking requirement in WebSocket frames, and why does it exist?
**Answer:** RFC 6455 mandates that every frame sent from client to server MUST be XOR-masked with a 4-byte masking key (randomly generated per frame and included in the header). Server-to-client frames must NOT be masked. The masking key is included in the frame header in plaintext, so masking is NOT a security feature (anyone can unmask). Its purpose is to defend against cache-poisoning attacks on intermediary HTTP caches that existed in the wild when WebSockets were standardized. The attack: a malicious script in a browser could craft a payload that looks like an HTTP GET request to a different URL (e.g., `GET /evil HTTP/1.1\r\n...`); an intermediary caching proxy inspecting the WebSocket stream might interpret this as a real HTTP request and poison its cache. By XOR-masking every client-to-server frame with a random key, the on-wire bytes look random to any intermediary that doesn't implement the WebSocket unmasking step, defeating the attack. The asymmetry (clients mask, servers don't) reflects that servers are trusted to not attempt cache-poisoning attacks. The mask is cheap (XOR with a 4-byte rotating key) and provides defense-in-depth. This is a subtle but important protocol design lesson: WebSocket could have just sent unmasked bytes, but the IETF added masking because real-world intermediaries (caches, proxies, firewalls) cannot be trusted to behave correctly.
**Visual:**
```
client -> server frame:
  +----+----+----+----+----+----+ ... +----+
  |hdr |MASK| k0 | k1 | k2 | k3 |     |p[n]^k[n%4]
  +----+----+----+----+----+----+ ... +----+
  payload bytes XORed with rotating 4-byte key

server -> client frame:
  +----+----+ ... +----+
  |hdr |len |     |payload (plaintext)
  +----+----+ ... +----+
```

### Q7. How do you handle back-pressure when a WebSocket client is slower than the server's push rate?
**Answer:** Back-pressure arises when the server produces events faster than the client can consume them — for example, a live trading feed pushing 1000 ticks/second to a mobile phone on a slow 3G connection. Without back-pressure handling, the server's send buffer fills, the kernel TCP send queue fills, then the server's process memory grows as it queues more frames in user space, and eventually the server OOMs or the kernel drops the connection. The recipe for handling this: (1) **Per-connection send queue with high-water mark** — each connection has a bounded queue (say 1000 frames or 1 MB); when the queue is full, the server stops accepting new frames for that connection and applies a policy: drop oldest, drop newest, close the connection, or signal the application to slow down. (2) **Use non-blocking sends** — track the queue depth; if the kernel socket buffer is full, the send returns EAGAIN; buffer the frame in the user-space queue and retry on the next epoll/kqueue writable event. (3) **Application-level flow control** — for collaborative-editing apps like Figma, the server can send a "slow down" message and the client throttles its local edits; for streaming media, switch to a lower bitrate. (4) **Drop policy by message type** — presence updates (typing indicator) are dropped silently; chat messages are queued and never dropped; close the connection only as a last resort. Slack and Discord both cap per-connection send queues and proactively close pathological clients. The general principle is the same as in Kafka consumer back-pressure (Phase 6): bounded buffers, explicit drop policies, and observable queue depth.
**Visual:**
```
producer (1000 msg/s) --> [server]
                          |
                          v
                    +-----------+      kernel TCP send buffer
                    | per-conn  | -->  (auto flow control)  -->  slow client
                    | queue     |                              (50 msg/s)
                    | HWM 1000  |
                    +-----------+
                          |
                    if queue full:
                      - drop presence/typing (low priority)
                      - queue chat messages (high priority)
                      - if chat queue also full -> close 1008
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You are designing WhatsApp's real-time delivery layer. Why WebSockets, and how do you avoid losing messages when a phone reconnects?
**Answer:** WhatsApp uses WebSockets (over TLS on port 443 to sidestep restrictive networks) because chat is bidirectional — the phone sends messages and the server pushes incoming messages, often within the same second. Polling would add 1-30s of latency; SSE would work for incoming but require a separate HTTP POST for outgoing, doubling complexity. WebSockets give one persistent full-duplex connection with sub-second push latency. To avoid losing messages on reconnect, the design is: (1) **Server-side per-user message queue** — every incoming message for an offline user is persisted in a per-user queue (backed by Cassandra or a similar store) with a monotonically increasing sequence number per conversation. (2) **Sequence numbers on every pushed frame** — each frame the server sends to the client carries a `seq` field; the client acks the highest seq it has durably processed (written to its local SQLite). (3) **On reconnect** — the client opens a fresh WebSocket and sends the last-acked seq per conversation; the server replays any queued messages with higher seq and then resumes live push. (4) **Idempotency** — message IDs are server-generated UUIDs, so a redelivered message is deduplicated by the client. (5) **Heartbeats** — ping/pong every 30s; if the server misses two pongs it considers the client offline, queues new messages, and waits for reconnect. This pattern is essentially how Slack, Discord, and Microsoft Teams all handle delivery-on-reconnect.
**Visual:**
```
phone disconnects at seq=42
  server queues: seq 43 "u there?", seq 44 "ping"
phone reconnects:
  phone --> CONNECT {last_seq: 42}
  server --> REPLAY seq 43, seq 44
  server --> LIVE   seq 45 (just arrived)
  phone --> ACK 45
  server deletes 43-45 from queue
```

### Q2. Your Slack-style chat app has grown to 10M concurrent WebSocket connections. Walk me through the architecture.
**Answer:** At 10M concurrent connections you cannot hold them all on one server, so the architecture is layered. (1) **Edge / TLS termination** — Cloudflare or AWS ALB terminates TLS at edge PoPs, keeping TLS handshake latency low for users worldwide and absorbing DDoS. The edge then opens a long-lived TCP connection to a backend WebSocket gateway. (2) **Sharded WebSocket gateways** — 50-100 gateway nodes, each holding ~100k-200k connections (Discord hit ~1M per Elixir node, but more conservative sizing is 100k for Python/Go). A consistent-hash router maps each user_id to a specific gateway shard; reconnecting clients use a session cookie so they land on the same shard holding their state. (3) **Per-node connection registry** — each gateway keeps an in-memory map of user_id -> socket; this is the source of truth for "which socket do I push to for user X on this node". (4) **Redis or Kafka pub/sub fan-out** — when any backend service wants to push to user X, it publishes to channel `user:X`; every gateway subscribes to the channels for users it currently owns; the owning gateway delivers to the socket. (5) **State store** — Redis (or ScyllaDB) holds user session, channel subscriptions, and last-ack seq so a reconnecting user on a different shard can resume. (6) **Heartbeats** — ping every 30s, idle timeout 90s; missed pongs trigger socket close. (7) **Draining** — when a gateway is decommissioned, the router stops sending it new connections, the gateway sends `1001 Going Away` close frames, clients reconnect, and the new shard fetches session from Redis. Total memory: ~50-100 KB per socket × 10M = 500 GB - 1 TB across the gateway fleet, plus Redis for sessions.
**Visual:**
```
10M clients
   |
  TLS edge (Cloudflare, AWS ALB)
   |
  consistent-hash router (user_id -> shard)
   |
  50 gateway shards (200k conns each)
   |  each gateway: in-memory user_id -> socket map
   |
  Redis pub/sub (channel per user, per channel)
   |
  backend services (message ingest, presence, typing)
```

### Q3. A corporate proxy is stripping the WebSocket Upgrade headers, breaking your app. What do you do?
**Answer:** Some corporate forward proxies (Zscaler, Blue Coat, McAfee Web Gateway, older Squid) inspect HTTP traffic and strip or modify unknown headers like `Upgrade: websocket`, causing the handshake to fail with a 200 OK that isn't an upgrade or a 403. Mitigations, in order of preference: (1) **Use `wss://` on port 443** — TLS encrypts the entire handshake, so the proxy cannot see or strip headers; it can only see "this is TLS traffic to port 443" and typically passes it through (though deep-packet-inspection proxies with a corporate root CA can still intercept, in which case the TLS appears terminated at the proxy and the proxy re-originates — the proxy must itself support WebSockets to forward correctly, which most modern ones do). (2) **HTTP fallback to long polling or SSE** — if WebSockets are blocked entirely, fall back to SSE (still HTTP, often passes) or long polling (always passes). Slack, Discord, and WhatsApp all have a polling or SSE fallback that the client automatically negotiates when the WebSocket fails. (3) **Use HTTP/2 with the WebSocket-over-HTTP/2 extension (RFC 8441)** — some modern proxies allow extended CONNECT over HTTP/2. (4) **Use a TURN/relay server** — for browser apps behind very restrictive networks, route traffic through a relay that the corporate proxy permits. (5) **Documentation** — document the proxy requirements (allow `Upgrade` and `Connection` headers, allow `101 Switching Protocols` response, allow long-lived idle connections) for IT administrators. The pragmatic answer is: ship WebSocket for the 95% of users where it works, ship a polling/SSE fallback for the 5% where it doesn't, and let the client auto-detect.
**Visual:**
```
attempt 1: ws://app.com  -> proxy strips Upgrade -> 200 OK (broken)
attempt 2: wss://app.com -> TLS hides headers    -> 101 (works, 95%)
attempt 3 (corporate MITM): proxy re-originates  -> if proxy supports WS, ok
                                                          else fallback
fallback:    GET /poll  -> long polling (always works)
```

### Q4. Your WebSocket server is hitting 100% CPU at 50k connections. How do you diagnose?
**Answer:** 50k connections is far below what a single WebSocket server should handle (Go and Erlang routinely do 100k-1M per node), so something is wrong. Diagnosis: (1) **Profile** — `py-spy` for Python, `pprof` for Go, `perf top` for native — find the hot function. Common culprits: per-frame UTF-8 validation (Python's websockets library validates every text frame), per-message JSON parsing, or accidentally doing O(n) work on every connection (e.g., iterating all 50k sockets to broadcast). (2) **Check the broadcast pattern** — if the server broadcasts to all 50k sockets on every message (a chat room with everyone subscribed), the per-message work is O(n) connections × per-frame encode cost; at 100 messages/second × 50k connections that's 5M frame encodes/second, which will peg a single CPU. Fix: shard the broadcast across worker threads/processes, or move to a fan-out tree where intermediate nodes aggregate. (3) **Check ping/pong frequency** — if pings are sent every 1 second to every connection, that's 50k frame encodes/second just for heartbeats; space pings to 30s. (4) **Check the event loop** — in Python, the GIL means a single event loop cannot use multiple cores; you must run multiple processes (one per core) and share connections across them via SO_REUSEPORT. (5) **Check JSON parse cost** — switching from JSON to a binary format like MessagePack or Protobuf can cut CPU by 3-5x. Discord's migration from Python to Elixir was driven largely by these exact bottlenecks; they hit ~70k connections per Python node before CPU saturation. The fix is usually: profile, shard, switch to a faster encoding, and use all cores.
**Visual:**
```
single Python process, 1 core, GIL
  50k conns, broadcast on every msg
  CPU pegged at 100%
  
diagnose:
  py-spy -> hot in json.loads + utf-8 validate
  every msg: 50k frame encodes + 50k json parses
  
fix:
  - move to 8 processes (SO_REUSEPORT) -> 8x cores
  - replace JSON with MessagePack        -> 3x faster parse
  - shard broadcast tree                 -> O(log n) not O(n)
  - space pings to 30s                   -> 30x less heartbeat work
  result: ~1M conns per box (8 cores)
```

### Q5. You need to push a single breaking-news notification to all 10M online users. How do you avoid a thundering herd?
**Answer:** Naive approach — broadcast to every socket immediately — would cause a 10M-message spike that overwhelms the gateway fleet and downstream services. The recipe: (1) **Stagger the send** — split the 10M users into batches of 100k-500k and send each batch over 1-2 seconds, spreading total delivery over 30-60 seconds. Users won't perceive a 30-second delay for a breaking news push, but the infrastructure stays stable. (2) **Per-connection rate limit** — gateways enforce a max sends-per-second per connection (e.g., 5/s); a broadcast that exceeds this gets queued and dripped out. (3) **Tiered priority** — breaking-news notifications are not chat messages; they can be dropped if a user is already saturated, and re-delivered on next reconnect. (4) **Coalesce** — if multiple notifications are pending for the same user within a 1-second window, merge them into one frame. (5) **Back-pressure observability** — monitor per-gateway queue depth; if depth exceeds HWM, throttle the broadcast producer or shed load. (6) **Push via a separate tier** — use Apple APNs / Google FCM for mobile push (which Apple/Google handle at their scale) for offline users, and reserve the WebSocket for users actively in the app. Twitter's live-tweet push, Instagram's live-story notifications, and Slack's @channel all stagger their broadcasts to avoid this exact problem. The general principle: never synchronously fan out to millions of sockets — always queue and drip.
**Visual:**
```
naive:    server -> 10M sockets simultaneously    (spike, OOM)

stagger:  server -> batch 1 (500k) at t=0
                   batch 2 (500k) at t=2s
                   batch 3 (500k) at t=4s
                   ...
                   batch 20 (500k) at t=40s   (smooth, queue depth < HWM)

per-conn: gateway enforces 5 frames/sec max per socket
coalesce: 3 notifications in 1s window -> 1 merged frame
```

### Q6. You are designing a multiplayer game server. WebSockets or UDP, and why?
**Answer:** Most browser-based multiplayer games use WebSockets because the browser WebSocket API is the only low-latency bidirectional option available (raw UDP is not exposed to JavaScript; WebRTC data channels are UDP-based but more complex). The trade-off: WebSockets run over TCP, which provides reliable in-order delivery but suffers from head-of-line blocking — a single dropped packet stalls all subsequent messages until retransmission succeeds, which can add 100-300 ms of latency on lossy mobile networks. For turn-based games (chess, card games), this is fine — WebSockets are perfect. For fast-paced shooters or racing games where 100 ms of stall is unacceptable and stale updates can simply be dropped (the next position update is more important than retransmitting the old one), UDP would be preferable, but the browser doesn't expose it. Workarounds: (1) **WebRTC data channels** — UDP-based, browser-supported, but requires signaling and is more complex to scale. (2) **Multiple WebSocket connections** — open 2-3 connections and send critical state updates on all; if one stalls, the others get through. (3) **Application-level staleness** — tag each position update with a timestamp; the client ignores updates older than the latest received, so a delayed retransmission is harmless. Real-world: Discord voice uses WebRTC (UDP-based Opus over RTP); browser games like slither.io use WebSockets; native games like Fortnite use raw UDP. The pragmatic browser choice is WebSocket with careful application-level handling of stale updates.
**Visual:**
```
browser game options:
  raw UDP        -> not exposed to JS
  WebRTC data    -> UDP-based, complex signaling, P2P-oriented
  WebSocket      -> TCP-based, simple, ubiquitous, but HoL blocking

decision tree:
  turn-based game (chess, cards)         -> WebSocket (simple, reliable)
  realtime strategy (Starcraft-like)     -> WebSocket ( HoL OK at 10Hz)
  fast-paced shooter (Fortnite browser)  -> WebRTC or multi-WS + staleness
  voice/video                             -> WebRTC (Opus over RTP/UDP)
```

### Q7. Your team proposes using WebSockets for a public REST-style API. How do you respond?
**Answer:** Push back. WebSockets are the wrong tool for a request-response API for several reasons. (1) **Semantic mismatch** — REST is fundamentally request-response: client asks for a resource, server answers, done. WebSockets are bidirectional streams; forcing them into request-response means reinventing HTTP (request IDs, correlation, timeouts, error codes) inside the WebSocket, losing REST's tooling (curl, Postman, OpenAPI, caching proxies, CDNs). (2) **Caching** — HTTP responses are cacheable by URLs, ETags, and Cache-Control; WebSocket frames are not cacheable by intermediaries at all. (3) **Load balancing** — stateless HTTP backends can be scaled trivially with any L7 LB; WebSockets require sticky sessions, per-connection state, and pub/sub fan-out for any cross-connection broadcast. (4) **Debugging** — `curl https://api.example.com/users/42` works out of the box; debugging a WebSocket requires a custom client. (5) **Standards** — REST has universal conventions (status codes, methods, headers); WebSockets have no conventions for request-response. Use WebSockets only for genuinely bidirectional or server-push use cases (chat, live dashboards, multiplayer, collaborative editing). For public APIs, use REST (or GraphQL) over HTTP. If you need both (e.g., GitHub: REST API for CRUD + WebSocket/SSE for live events), expose them as separate endpoints. The exception is gRPC, which uses HTTP/2 streams for request-response but with a formal contract — that's a different beast from raw WebSockets.
**Visual:**
```
wrong:   client --ws--> server     (request-response over WS)
         reinvents: msg_id, correlation, timeout, status codes
         loses:     curl, caching, OpenAPI, L7 LB

right:   client --HTTP--> server   (REST for CRUD)
         client --ws----> server   (only for live push, chat)
         both endpoints coexist
```

quiz.explanation: Long polling** — client sends HTTP GET, server holds the request open up to 30s waiting for data, then responds; client immediately re-requests. Simple, works everywhere (even ancient proxies), but high overhead (fresh HTTP request per event batch, thread per held request on server), and high latency for the first event after a poll cycle.

quiz.question: What is the masking requirement in WebSocket frames, and why does it exist?
options: Text and binary are the data opcodes; close, ping, pong are control opcodes that must be processed even mid-fragmented-message.
Long polling** — client sends HTTP GET, server holds the request open up to 30s waiting for data, then responds; client immediately re-requests.

quiz.explanation: RFC 6455 mandates that every frame sent from client to server MUST be XOR-masked with a 4-byte masking key (randomly generated per frame and included in the header). Server-to-client frames must NOT be masked. The masking key is included in the frame header in plaintext, so masking is NOT a security feature (anyone can unmask).
